body.text: Most telling is what the report cannot say. Without strong data on costs and outcomes, its authors concede, there is no way to tell whether lower spending reflected genuine efficiency gains or simply less adequate assistance. Efficiency, in other words, is a claim the system cannot yet verify.

Rather than confront that gap, the system has redefined it. The United Nations’ 2026 appeals were billed as “hyper-prioritised”, built on a narrower definition of humanitarian need that made the shortfall look smaller, while aid workers warned that many people in need were simply no longer being counted.

At this year’s UN General Assembly in New York, which coincided with the release of the ALNAP report, international actors acknowledged they were doing less with less, yet were still patting each other on the back and preserving a system that is failing by almost every measurable indicator.

Meanwhile, the approaches proven to deliver better value went backwards. Cash and flexible multiyear funding work but the share of UN agencies and international NGOs giving multiyear funding to partners fell as organisations looked to efficiency.

Much of the “saving” has simply been shifted onto local organisations, their staff and people they serve. Local and national groups make up 81% of humanitarian organisations, and 94% of humanitarian staff are nationals of the countries where they work. Yet in 2025, local actors received just 4.3% of humanitarian funding directly, and national NGOs held 11% of seats on Humanitarian Country Teams, against 79% of UN agencies, international NGOs and donors.

The system also grades itself more generously than the people it serves. In 2025, 67% of practitioners rated their targeting of those in most urgent need as good or excellent; only 51% of aid recipients agreed, and just 53% said the assistance met their most important needs.
